Apple has filed its proposal for the fees it would charge on transactions not processed through the App Store system as part of the Epic Games lawsuit. Here are the details.

Apple Files Proposed Commission for Non-App Store Transactions

After multiple attempts to stay the district court hearing that will determine how much, if any, Apple can charge for transactions that bypass the App Store's IAP system, Apple has now filed its proposal laying out a suggested fee structure.

Apple's filing comes as the Supreme Court rejected the company's request to stay the lower court hearing; the Supreme Court is currently considering whether Apple can be found in contempt for charging a 27% commission on non-App Store transactions. The case stems from an injunction issued by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, which requires Apple to let developers direct users to alternative payment methods.

Apple has argued in both the lower court and the Supreme Court that the court's ruling could affect the outcome of the hearing on fee determinations, meaning that hearing should be stayed pending the court's decision. However, the Supreme Court rejected Apple's request, allowing the lower court hearing to proceed while it considers the matter.

Apple has therefore now filed its proposal, which recommends the following:

Standard apps would face a 15% fee (with these apps still paying the 30% in-app purchase (IAP) commission); Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP) and subscription renewals would face a 10% fee; apps under the Small Business Program would face a 5% fee.

According to Apple, "Factual and expert evidence on these proposed commission rates was filed concurrently." The company added:

Apple added that its "proposed external link commissions can also be compared to the commissions of other app stores that compete with the App Store," including Google Play, the Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted that "Google Play Store's external link fee rates are 20% for standard, 15% for programs, and 10% for subscriptions—and Epic agreed to these rates."

Apple said it still believes the hearing on fee determination should be stayed during the Supreme Court's review, adding that the filing was made only to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's directive.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket injunction on external link transaction commissions, noting that issues only arise when the commission effectively equates to a prohibition.

With the proposal filed, Epic will have an opportunity to respond, and Apple is expected to submit its brief to the Supreme Court by September 14.
